title: Healthier Salt Could Save Millions of Lives
paragraphs: Eating too much salt is known to raise blood pressure, which in turn increases the risk of heart disease and stroke. Now, a new study suggests that replacing ordinary salt with a healthier alternative could prevent nearly three million deaths around the world every year.

The study was led by researchers at The George Institute for Global Health in Australia. They focused on potassium-enriched salt, a type of salt in which part of the sodium chloride found in regular table salt is replaced with potassium chloride. It looks, tastes and cooks in much the same way as ordinary salt. It tackles two problems at once: consuming too much sodium and not getting enough potassium, both of which are well-established causes of high blood pressure.

Using computer modeling, the researchers estimated the potential health benefits across 193 countries. They calculated that if all salt worldwide were replaced with potassium-enriched salt, about 2.96 million deaths could be prevented each year, along with about 10.17 million new cases of cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease.

Even a partial switch could make a big difference. Replacing only the salt used in home cooking could prevent around 1.85 million deaths a year. The largest benefits would be seen in China, where about 1.08 million deaths could be prevented annually, followed by India, with almost 400,000.

However, the researchers acknowledged that a complete global switch is ambitious. In Europe and North America, more than 70% of the salt people eat comes from processed foods and restaurant meals, so the food industry would need to cooperate. In addition, the production of potassium chloride would need to increase substantially.

There are also safety concerns. People with advanced kidney disease, as well as those taking certain medications, could be at risk of having too much potassium in their blood, so they should consult a doctor first.

It is important to note that the figures are estimates from a model rather than results from a clinical trial. Nevertheless, the World Health Organization endorsed potassium-enriched salt in 2025 as a way to lower blood pressure.
